h1: Partnership disputes at a brewery and how to resolve them
title: Resolving Brewery Partner Disputes | Craft Beer School
desc: Why brewery partners fall out, the early warning signs and how to resolve a dispute through talks, mediation or a buyout before it reaches court.
teaser: Most brewery partnerships do not end over beer. They end over money, time and who gets the final say.
standfirst: Brewery partners fall out for predictable reasons. If you know what they are, read the signs early and use the agreement you already signed, most disputes can be settled without a lawyer's letter. This is general guidance, not legal advice.
sections: Most brewery fights are about money, time and control

Two friends open a brewpub, one puts in most of the cash and the other works on the floor six days a week. Two years later both feel they carry the business. That pattern sits behind a large share of brewery disputes. The usual triggers are easy to list:

  • A capital call when the build overruns and one partner cannot pay their share.
  • Uneven work: a full-time operating partner beside a part-time or silent one.
  • Control: who decides the beer list, the prices, the next hire or a second outlet.
  • Drawings: one partner needs a salary from the business while the other wants profit reinvested.
  • Exit: one partner wants to sell and the other does not.

A 50:50 split makes each of these worse, because nobody has a casting vote.

Disputes rarely start with a row. They start with drift. Partner meetings get skipped. Decisions sit for weeks. One partner stops reading the monthly numbers or starts questioning every expense. Staff begin asking which partner to listen to.

The cheapest protection is shared information. Agree that a monthly profit and loss statement and a bank reconciliation reach every partner by the 10th of the following month, prepared by the accountant rather than by one partner. Suspicion grows fastest where one person holds the books and the others hold opinions.

When tension shows, call a proper meeting, not a late-night chat at the bar. Put a written agenda on the table. Bring the last six months of accounts. Agree the facts first (cash in the bank, debts, what each partner has put in and taken out) before anyone discusses fairness.

Separate the business question from the personal one. "We need ₹10 lakh for a new fermenter and I cannot fund half" is a business question with several answers: a loan, a new investor, a change in shareholding or waiting a year. "You never pull your weight" is a feeling. Both matter, but the first can be solved on paper.
Bring in a neutral before a lawyer

If two or three meetings get nowhere, bring in someone both partners trust: an adviser, a board member, the company's chartered accountant or a trained mediator. Mediation is private and nothing is binding until both sides sign an agreement. It costs far less than a court case. Court cases in India can run for years while the brewery bleeds.

A good neutral asks each partner what they need, not what they demand. The operating partner may need a fair salary and a say in daily decisions. The investor may need a timeline for returns. Those needs often fit together once they are said out loud.
Use what the agreement already says

Before anyone threatens anything, read the documents you signed: the partnership deed, the LLP agreement or the shareholders' agreement. The structure matters. Our guide to choosing a company, LLP or partnership explains how each handles ownership. Look for:

  • A deadlock clause saying what happens when partners cannot agree.
  • A buy-sell or shotgun clause that lets one partner name a price and the other choose to buy or sell at it.
  • The valuation method for a partner's share.
  • A dispute clause naming mediation, arbitration or a jurisdiction.
  • Who owns the brand, the trademark and the recipes.

If these clauses are missing, that is the lesson for the next agreement. Our guide to brewery partner agreements covers what to put in. Have a lawyer read your existing documents before you act on them.
Keep the brewery running while you argue

Customers, staff and tanks do not stop for a partner dispute. Agree a ceasefire on operations: the head brewer keeps brewing to the agreed plan, salaries and excise duty get paid on time and neither partner makes a large decision alone while talks go on. A beer left too long in a fermenter at 20 °C does not care who is right.

Keep the dispute away from the floor. Staff who hear partners argue at the bar start looking for other jobs, usually the good ones first. Talk about it in an office, with the door shut.
When the answer is a buyout

Sometimes the fix is that one partner leaves. Valuing a brewery share is where many buyouts stall. The common approaches are net assets, a multiple of earnings or a price an independent valuer sets. Equipment is worth far less second hand than it cost new. A brewery licence generally sits with the entity and premises, not with a person. If ownership or directors change, check whether your state excise department needs to be told or must approve it.

A buyout paid in instalments over 12 to 24 months is often easier for a small brewery's cash flow than a lump sum. Tie each instalment to a date, not to profits the leaving partner can no longer influence.

Your first step: book the next partners' meeting with a written agenda and a shared profit and loss statement. Before that meeting, read your agreement's deadlock clause with your lawyer.
faqs: What is the most common cause of brewery partnership disputes?
Money and effort out of balance: one partner funds the business while another runs it. The two then disagree on salaries, drawings or new spending.
Mediation is not binding until both sides sign a settlement. Arbitration, if your agreement names it, produces a binding award. A lawyer can explain which applies to you.
Does a brewery licence pass to the remaining partner in a buyout?
Licences usually sit with the licensed entity and premises. Whether a change in partners or directors needs excise approval varies by state, so check the current rules.
